channel.title: LLM ThreatIntel
channel.description: Threat intelligence tracking malicious LLM tools, GenAI-assisted malware, supply chain compromises, LLMjacking operations, shadow AI risks, and nation-state GenAI adoption.

item.title: Italy and Switzerland Issue Warnings on Autonomous AI Agent Attacks Against Critical Infrastructure
item.description: According to BleepingComputer, Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies warned about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting critical infrastructure organizations. BleepingComputer reported that CSIRT Italia detected large scale malicious campaigns using autonomous AI agents to exploit exposed endpoints, and Switzerland's National Cyber Security Center confirmed its first cases of successful AI assisted cyberattacks against organizations in at least two sectors. The two agencies urged organizations to reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet, prioritize patching, and monitor for unusual activity.

item.title: Microsoft Details ARTEX Agentic AI Framework Abuse Across Secret Hunting, Supply Chain, and Internet Facing Exploitation
item.description: According to the Microsoft Security Blog, Microsoft Threat Intelligence published a November 25 post titled What defenders need to know about ARTEX, the agentic AI framework threat actors abuse. The title names ARTEX as an agentic AI framework that threat actors abuse, and the post is filed under Research. The captured source text provides only the page framing, with no campaign details or indicators, so no indicator values are reported here.

item.title: Wiz Links ARTEX Offensive AI Framework Activity to More Than a Dozen Organizations
item.description: Wiz reported that between late October and mid November 2026 it tied activity, at varying confidence, to more than a dozen organizations and observed routing through ISP proxy exit nodes spanning more than 220 IPs in a single target. The report provides independent vendor analysis of the ARTEX offensive AI framework that the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence already described. Defenders should treat proxy fan out across large IP sets within one target as a signal of automated offensive tooling and review outbound egress for proxy chains.

item.title: Unit 42 Tracks More Than 10 Autonomous AI Agent Campaigns Operating at Machine Speed
item.description: Unit 42 tracked more than 10 global campaigns between July and September 2026 in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents that compressed the attack lifecycle from weeks or days into hours. Every observed campaign began with a web shell planted through a vulnerable web application, and targets spanned government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture, and education. Defenders should prioritize web shell detection and hardening of internet facing web applications because the operators matched proficient human tradecraft while running hundreds of commands in minutes.

item.title: Darktrace Signal Labs Demonstrates Claude Code Memory Stores Abused as a Covert Command and Control Channel
item.description: Darktrace Signal Labs showed that Claude Code memory stores can be repurposed as a live command and control channel between external operators and AI agents running inside a corporate environment. The technique requires no flaw in the Claude platform and only stolen Claude Console API credentials; it was proven in a controlled lab and has not been observed in the wild. Defenders should monitor agent harness process creation and network traffic against behavioral baselines, because the channel rides the same API endpoint used for normal inference.

item.title: Google Threat Intelligence Group Says Agentic Threat Activity Crossed a Significant Threshold
item.description: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that adversary use of autonomous agentic tooling has crossed a significant threshold, including autonomous multi agent frameworks, automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes. The update spans cyber crime and state linked activity. Defenders should assume agentic offensive operations are now sustained rather than experimental.

item.title: AhnLab Reports 40,000 Exposed OpenClaw Agent Instances and Hundreds of Malicious Skills
item.description: AhnLab's AI Threat Trends Report states that 40,000 OpenClaw agent instances were found exposed on the internet and 35.4 percent of them were classified as vulnerable. An audit of one Skill marketplace found that 341 Skills were malicious. Defenders running OpenClaw or similar agent frameworks should locate and restrict internet exposed instances and vet marketplace Skills before agents load them.

item.title: OX Security Finds Agent Skills and MCP Servers Weaponized for Instruction Based Supply Chain Attacks
item.description: OX Security analyzed 542,207 open source components across npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills between July and October 2026 and found that attackers can now hijack agents through malicious instructions rather than executable code. Prompt injection and tool poisoning appeared in 22 percent of flagged MCP servers, and 44 percent of flagged Agent Skills contained instructions directing agents to send data out without executing code at install time. Defenders should treat MCP server and Skill trust signals as broken and verify component provenance and runtime behavior before agents connect.

item.title: Microsoft Security Documents Device Code Phishing That Can Steer AI Coding Agents Remotely
item.description: Microsoft Security showed in a lab simulation that a phished OAuth device code authorization for an AI coding agent can let an attacker steer an active GitHub Copilot CLI session, run commands on the victim machine, poison agent memory, read cloud synced sessions, and reach private repositories. The technique is not specific to GitHub and works against any public client that supports the device flow, with the attacker choosing the requested scopes. Defenders should restrict device code flow for agent clients, require conditional access, and alert on device code sign ins for coding agents.

item.title: Dragos Canary Experiment Exposes Prompt Theft and Data Leakage Across the AI Inference Supply Chain
item.description: A Dragos researcher seeded nearly 2 million prompts with unique trackable secrets and found at least three AI providers compromised by attackers who siphoned prompts, multiple resellers that leaked prompts, and providers that ignored zero data retention flags. Stolen AWS keys were reused tens of thousands of times in AWS API calls, and a Chinese AI lab scraped secret URLs even from requests marked no data collection. Enterprises should treat any prompt sent to an external model provider as potentially disclosed and rotate every credential that has transited a third party inference endpoint.

item.title: AWS Reports Chinese Nexus Cairn AI Agents Autonomously Discovered and Exploited a Zero Day in a Medical Imaging AI Application
item.description: Amazon Threat Intelligence disclosed that a Chinese nexus operator running the open source autonomous penetration testing framework Cairn left an instance exposed without authentication, revealing a campaign in which AI agents found and exploited an unpatched zero day on their own. The agents achieved root level shell access on a medical imaging AI application in about 11 minutes via a path traversal upload parameter, then planted a Python reverse shell through sitecustomize.py. Defenders running the affected open source medical imaging project should apply the vendor fix and review Python startup file integrity and training API endpoint exposure.

item.title: Pluto Security Skill2Exploit Delivers Nextcloud Zero Day RCE Through a Harmless AI Agent Skill
item.description: Pluto Security disclosed Skill2Exploit, a technique where a benign looking AI agent skill fetches a crafted file that exploits a vulnerability in another service, triggering remote code execution with no malicious code in the skill itself. They proved it with a zero day RCE in Nextcloud's HEIC preview path via the libde265 decoder, affecting any instance running a pre November 6 2026 image with HEIC preview enabled. Administrators should move to a current fpm-alpine image (Nextcloud 32 to 35) or an Alpine 3.24 build and review how agents fetch and process untrusted files.

item.title: CrowdStrike Warns Backdoored LoRA Models Enable Supply Chain Compromise of AI Agents
item.description: CrowdStrike researchers detailed how cheap Low-Rank Adaptation fine tunes of open weight models can carry conditional backdoors that pass standard benchmarks and stay dormant until a trigger phrase or date appears. ProjectDiscovery demonstrated a $50 LoRA fine tune of Qwen2.5-7B that emits a tool call to an attacker controlled URL whenever a trigger phrase entered a prompt, and any agent that auto dispatches tool calls will execute it. Defenders should treat model weights from third parties and internal teams as untrusted code and add independent observability over agent tool calls.

item.title: Bitdefender Labs Documents GitHub Malware Campaign Hiding Payloads in AI Agent Instruction Files
item.description: Bitdefender Labs identified 22 malicious GitHub links that conceal payloads inside the files and automation configurations AI coding assistants read when they join a project. The malware can steal developer credentials, cloud secrets, CI/CD tokens, package registry credentials, browser data, and password manager data, then plant fresh AI agent instructions to keep spreading. Defenders should treat agent instruction files, session start hooks, MCP configurations, and editor task files as untrusted code and scan developer workstations for unauthorized edits to them.

item.title: Google Threat Intelligence Group Observes PentAGI and CAIRN Multi Agent Frameworks Deployed in the Wild and CyberStrikeAI in Experimentation
item.description: Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that agentic threat activity crossed a significant threshold, with the open source multi agent frameworks CAIRN and PentAGI independently observed deployed in real intrusions and CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI seen in threat actor experimentation. These frameworks share autonomous target discovery and exploitation capabilities that lower the skill barrier for offensive operations. Defenders should monitor environments for multi agent framework traffic and unexpected agent tool invocation.

item.title: FBI FLASH Advisory Warns ARTEX Autonomous Pentest Framework Driving Global Attacks and ConnectWise Supply Chain Breach
item.description: The FBI issued a FLASH advisory warning that multiple threat actors have weaponized the ARTEX autonomous penetration testing framework since at least August 2026 to automate intrusions across financial, government, technology, defense, and healthcare sectors, including a ConnectWise supply chain breach that compromised Microsoft 365 customer environments. ARTEX chains techniques fast enough to move from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours, and researchers counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles as of early November. Defenders should hunt for the framework's high volume reconnaissance traffic and review third party integration portals that ARTEX targets effectively.

item.title: Google Threat Intelligence Group Documents exploit_agent Framework Fully Automating Patch Differential Analysis Into Live Exploitation
item.description: Google Threat Intelligence Group reported the first observed case of threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop, via a multi agent staging server it dubbed exploit_agent. The framework runs continuous differential analysis of web application patches, drafts exploits, and executes them against internet facing servers automatically, and victim telemetry points to interest in French media, entertainment, and education targets. Defenders should treat agentic exploitation pipelines as an active capability, not a theoretical one, and prioritize rapid patch application on internet facing infrastructure.

item.title: Cursor Update Traces Claude Code Marketplace Tampering to Exposed Fireworks Access Key and Unredacted Agent Trace Credentials
item.description: Cursor's November 13 incident update states the October 29 attack began when Fireworks exposed an access key issued by Cursor, which the attacker used to copy data from a read only storage bucket holding coding agent traces that contained unredacted credentials for less than 0.01 percent of customers. The attacker then reached internal SaaS tools, archived non production source repositories, support data, and credentials, and used a stolen credential to place malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace cache, potentially served to at most 5,000 users for about 11 hours. Developers who installed or updated Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the Cursor marketplace during the exposure window should follow Cursor's remediation steps, since uninstalling the extension alone may not be sufficient.

item.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence Documents ARTEX Agents Running Self Sustaining AI Credential Theft and Deepfake KYC Fraud Campaigns
item.description: Amazon Threat Intelligence observed threat actors using the open source ARTEX agentic AI penetration testing framework to run sustained offensive campaigns between October 3 and November 5, 2026, captured by the MadPot decoy sensor network. The most prominent campaign stole AI provider API keys at scale and recycled them to pay for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting, while another targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for KYC verification bypass using real time deepfake injection. Organizations exposing AI inference endpoints or hosting upstream provider keys in internet facing applications should audit credential exposure and monitor for agentic request patterns against their LLM APIs.

item.title: Microsoft research shows dataset and model poisoning backdoors hijack coding agents at up to 94.8 percent success
item.description: Microsoft Security Blog reported that dataset poisoning during fine tuning and model poisoning of open weight checkpoints can backdoor coding agents, with attack success up to 94.8 percent on unseen repositories. The research shows that in distribution evaluations can overstate backdoor robustness and that hidden triggers can cause agents to invoke command execution tools. Defenders should audit model provenance, diff weights against original checkpoints, and monitor agent tool calls for unexpected behavior.
